source.title: Counting in Small Transformers: The Delicate Interplay between Attention and Feed-Forward Layers
source.authors: Freya Behrens; Luca Biggio; Lenka Zdeborová

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results on token-embedding overlap and counting with embedding dimension below alphabet size. These refine the scope of the overlap-and-interference account, but do not test feature sparsity or importance.
record.gate_note: The paper measures embedding overlaps and counting accuracy in toy transformer models, including when d < T. It does not vary feature activation sparsity or feature importance. Its LLM counting results assess counting behavior, not feature geometry or SAE recovery, so they are not rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It trains 1-layer transformers on a histogram (counting) task. When embedding dimension d < alphabet size T, token embeddings are necessarily non-orthogonal. That is a geometric fact of the embedding layer, not an emergent storage choice under sparsity or importance. The paper never varies feature sparsity or importance, never tests a sparsity-dependent transition, and never examines whether features are stored in superposition as in the toy model. 'Superposition' appears only in related work and in the sense of two algorithms implemented together. The overlap and interference results concern a related construct (counting robustness to embedding coherence), so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that counting solutions (relation-based vs inventory-based) depend on mixing mechanism, feed-forward width, embedding dimension and softmax. When d < T, non-orthogonal embeddings entangle count information. Discreteness of counts and softmax attention give robustness to this noise, with hand constructions reaching d = 7 for T = 32.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and analyzes small transformer variants on a histogram task and supplies theoretical constructions; it does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Embedding dimension, feed-forward width, token-mixing architecture, softmax, sequence length, and whether embeddings are learned affect accuracy or robustness.

fits_no_version.finding: In 1-layer transformers with d < T, learned token embeddings overlap. Smaller d gives overcounting and lower accuracy (57.71% at d=3, 87.67% at d=8, 98.28% at d=23 for dot). Because the task is discrete, near-perfect solutions still exist below d=T. Softmax attention tolerates more embedding coherence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interference from non-orthogonal token embeddings (d < T) degrades algorithmic task accuracy in a way that discrete outputs and softmax can absorb. The tolerable mutual coherence is bounded via the Welch bound.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML); proceedings stated as PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The toy models are simplified, non-autoregressive, and omit causal masks and positional embeddings. Several overlap and accuracy values are presented only in figures. The paper notes large initialization variability in some regimes and weaker performance for longer sequences; its low-dimensional perfect constructions are not learned.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional architecture and hyperparameter accuracy sweeps in Figs. 1–2 and appendices, but these do not separately measure the overlap geometry relevant to V1. LLM counting evaluations in Figs. 6–7 concern task performance, not feature representation. No claim-version-specific results from these were added as rows.

untested.parts: Sparsity-dependent transition, the role of feature importance, near-orthogonal storage arising under sparsity, and regular geometry. Token-embedding overlap is forced when d < T, so it does not test these.
All parts: polysemantic neurons and capacity competition.
All parts. The LLM counting evaluations (App. A) measure task accuracy only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/tests classification is overridden. The paper is about counting algorithms in small transformers. Its d < T regime makes embedding overlap unavoidable rather than an emergent superposition finding, and it cites Toy Models of Superposition only in passing. The random-but-fixed embedding comparison (App. E.3) shows learned embeddings beat random ones when d < T. This is suggestive of adapted geometry but is not a superposition measurement.

versions.untested_parts: Does not vary feature sparsity or importance, test a sparsity-dependent transition, or establish regular geometry of sparse features. Its objects are token embeddings in a histogram task.
Polysemantic neurons, feature competition for capacity, and dedicated versus shared feature dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise without capacity pressure.
Feature distribution across neurons in LLMs and recovery of sparse features by dictionaries or SAEs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.
Whether model features are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

rows.subject: dot
rows.operation_detail: Measured same-token and different-token embedding overlap distributions and histogram accuracy.
rows.note: The text says smaller d gives a less spread overlap distribution and overcounting. The plotted overlap values are not stated in text.
rows.check: Overlap among T > d embeddings is forced by dimensionality, not a measured superposition outcome. Sparsity and importance are not varied. Accuracy 57.71% is counting accuracy, not a superposition measure.

rows.subject: dot, trained embeddings
rows.size_stated: T = 32, L = 10; d varies as in Fig. 5; p = 32
rows.operation_detail: Compared overlap distributions for embeddings of same and different tokens across embedding dimensions.
rows.measure: Spread of same-token and different-token embedding overlaps
rows.value: The text reports less spread in the overlap distribution for smaller d; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The paper describes non-orthogonal embeddings and overlap-induced count entanglement; it does not state that the learned directions are nearly orthogonal.
rows.check: The text says only that smaller d gives 'a less spread distribution of overlaps' and overcounting. There is no sparsity manipulation and no test of near-orthogonality or regular geometry. This is a related construct.

rows.subject: bos+sftm
rows.operation_detail: Constructed binary-representation token embeddings and selected a softmax inverse temperature to preserve discrete count margins.
rows.note: The paper says these constructions are not learned; this is a theoretical existence result, not a trained-model result.
rows.check: A hand-built theoretical construction (Prop. 4.5), not a learned model. The paper states these are not learned. It should not be an empirical result row.

rows.subject: dot+sftm
rows.operation_detail: Constructed token embeddings and used softmax to reduce effects of non-equal-token similarities.
rows.note: The construction is stated for d ≥ ceil(log2(T + 1)) + 2; the paper gives d = 7 for T = 32. It is not a learned model.
rows.check: A hand-built construction (Prop. 4.5, App. C.3.2), not learned. It should not be an empirical result row.
